technical_and_design_decisions: Use Go modules with 'replace' directives in go.mod pointing to the Fabric repository (at a pinned commit/tag) to externalize the previously inlined packages.

Strategy for SDK-specific modifications found in the copied code: prefer to upstream minor fixes/enhancements back to Fabric; for changes that cannot be upstreamed in time, keep them as thin SDK-local wrappers/extensions instead of forking the package.

Order the externalizations so that foundational packages (common utilities, ledger base interfaces) are migrated before packages that depend on them (ccprovider, configtxgen, configtxlator), to avoid large broken intermediate states.
Preserve the public Go API of the SDK unchanged; refactor only internal/SDK-side imports and call sites so that SDK consumers are not impacted.

Treat U6 (go.mod handling in chaincode packages) as a narrow, feature-flagged workaround behind a configuration option, with TODOs and a deprecation note to ensure it is removed once the broader transition completes.
Reuse the existing unit and integration test suites as the primary regression safety net; add targeted tests only where new wrapper/extension code is introduced.
Update CI/CD scripts and linters to recognize the new import paths and to ensure the SDK can be built and tested with Go modules against the external Fabric dependency.
assumptions: The developer performing the work has prior, hands-on experience with the Hyperledger Fabric Go SDK and with Fabric's internal package layout, so discovery and impact analysis are relatively fast.
Fabric publishes stable, semver-tagged Go modules (or a stable branch) that can be consumed by the SDK during this effort.
Most of the 'modifications' in the SDK's internal/third_party copies are small and limited; deep refactors of upstream behavior are not required.
The ledger externalization (U4) covers only the ledger subpackages actually imported by the SDK today, not the entire Fabric ledger implementation.
No major breaking API changes are introduced upstream in Fabric during the development window; otherwise an additional buffer would be needed.

Time spent on asynchronous code review iterations, waiting for upstream merges, and release coordination is not included in the most-likely effort; the estimate covers the developer's own active work only.
A standard 1 work-hour ≈ 1 effective engineering hour is assumed (no meeting overhead, no context-switching losses), since the request is for software development effort, not elapsed duration.

activities.activity_description: Survey the current SDK tree, enumerate every file under internal/github.com/hyperledger/fabric and third_party/github.com/hyperledger/fabric, identify the upstream package each file came from, and record the SDK-specific deltas. Produce a design document describing the externalization order, replacement strategy, and handling of SDK-specific modifications.

Update the SDK's go.mod to add the Fabric module as an external dependency, configure 'replace' directives pointing to the target Fabric commit/tag, and update Makefile/CI scripts so the build and vet/test stages work with the new module graph.

Remove the SDK-local copy of the gossip protoext utilities from internal/github.com/hyperledger/fabric/gossip, redirect imports to the external Fabric package, reconcile any SDK-specific changes in the discovery client with upstream behavior, and rerun gossip/discovery unit tests.

Remove the third_party copy of common/cauthdsl, switch the SDK to import cauthdsl from the external Fabric module, adapt any consumers (e.g., policy creation/evaluation in the SDK) to the upstream API, and re-run policy-related tests.

Remove the third_party copy of core/common/ccprovider, import ccprovider from the external Fabric module, update chaincode install/instantiate flows in the SDK to use the upstream structures (CCPackage, CDSPackage, etc.), and verify chaincode packaging tests still pass.

Remove the third_party copy of the ledger-related packages used by the SDK, switch SDK imports to the external Fabric ledger module, resolve any interface or behavior differences (especially around the ledger interfaces the SDK depends on for query results and block retrieval), and run ledger/query integration tests.

Remove the SDK-local copies under internal/github.com/hyperledger/fabric/common and internal/github.com/hyperledger/fabric/core, redirect SDK imports to the external Fabric common packages, port any SDK-specific modifications into thin SDK-local extensions where needed, and run the full common-related test suite.

Remove the SDK-local copy of sdkinternal/configtxgen and the corresponding code in pkg/fab/resource/configtx.go, import configtxgen from the external Fabric module, adapt the resource manager to the upstream API for channel/profiles/genesis-block creation, and re-run channel-creation integration tests.

Remove the SDK-local copy of sdkinternal/configtxlator, import configtxlator from the external Fabric module, update SDK callers (proto/config conversions used by the resource manager) to the upstream API, and validate with config-translation unit and integration tests.

Implement a temporary, opt-in workaround that recognizes a go.mod file included in a chaincode package during build/dependency resolution. Gate it behind a configuration flag, add unit tests covering presence/absence of go.mod, and add a clear deprecation/TODO comment explaining it is short-lived.

Run the full SDK unit test suite, the integration tests against a local Fabric network, and end-to-end scenarios (channel creation, chaincode install/instantiate/invoke, gossip discovery, ledger queries, config translation) to confirm no regressions from the externalizations.

Update README, CONTRIBUTING, and architecture docs to reflect the new externalized dependencies, document the temporary go.mod chaincode workaround (and its deprecation), and note that the SDK now tracks a specific Fabric version for these packages.
